how-much-to-charge-for-artificial-turf.h.text:
← Artificial turf bid calculator

How much to charge for artificial turf

A published $8-a-square-foot special treats 600 square feet of landscape turf on a prepared pad as the same job as 800 square feet of pet turf with sod demo, a 4-inch crushed-rock base, zeolite infill, and two tree wells. It is not. Lawn-care calculators price a recurring mow on living grass. Paver and concrete calculators price hardscape. Installing synthetic turf is a type, a waste factor, and the extra work you have to do before the first roll goes down. Quoting all of that from a per-square-foot special is how the first odor callback eats the field margin.

A job with the same square footage can cost much more

Turf you buy is larger than the lawn because rolls are 15 feet wide. On the sample rates a 600-square-foot landscape job with 10% waste, a 3-inch base, and sod demo prices about $5,468 ($9.11 per square foot, 22.2 crew-hours, 660 sq ft of turf to buy, walk-away $3,828). The same shop’s 800-square-foot pet yard with a 4-inch base and two tree wells prices about $11,124 ($13.90 per square foot, 36.5 hours, 896 sq ft to buy). About a third of that pet bid is extra work — thicker base, zeolite, drainage, and the wells. Matching the landscape job’s $9.11-a-square-foot number on the pet yard is how that job becomes a loss.

Landscape looks cheaper until the yard is a pet yard

Landscaping a pet yard is a callback, not a savings. On the same 800-square-foot lawn the sample rates price landscape turf at about $7,225 — $3,899 less than pet. That gap is drainage and odor-grade infill, not profit. Putting-green of that run prices about $12,639. Landscape is still the right bid on a 600-square-foot refresh that only needed a 3-inch base: pet on that refresh prices higher because you would be buying zeolite for a yard that only needed sand. Treating every lawn as one per-square-foot number is how the type that looked cheapest on paper is not the one that keeps the margin.

A putting green is not automatically the cheap small job

A 400-square-foot putting green with 15% waste and 80 feet of seam is not a 600-square-foot landscape job minus 200 square feet. On the sample rates that putting green prices about $7,107 ($17.77 per square foot, 26.1 crew-hours, 460 sq ft to buy). Extra seams and a 4.5-inch base are their own tickets. A 1,200-square-foot landscape job on a new pad (no sod) prices about $9,621 ($8.02 per square foot). Neither number lives in an $8-a-square-foot special.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $32/h hand loaded at 30% payroll burden is $41.60. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. An $8-a-square-foot quote on the 800-square-foot pet yard is $6,400 against a $7,787 walk-away. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is arithmetic on the rates you type. It is not a landscaping specification, a drainage design, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommendation of landscape versus pet turf. Base condition, drainage, and what the homeowner will accept still decide the type. Verify every figure against your own takeoff.

No warranty. This free page is not landscaping, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. It is hosted best-effort with no SLA: it may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Open the bid calculator to price a specific lawn.

Common questions

How much to charge for artificial turf?

Charge from the turf type (landscape, pet, or putting-green), the lawn square footage, roll waste, crushed-rock base depth, sod demo, infill, seams, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 600-square-foot landscape job with 10% waste, a 3-inch base, and sod demo at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $5,468 — about $9.11 per square foot.

When is pet turf more than a landscape special?

When the yard needs zeolite or antimicrobial infill, extra drainage, a thicker base, and sod demo. On the sample rates an 800-square-foot pet yard with two tree wells prices around $11,124. Landscaping that same yard prices around $7,225. The per-square-foot special never sees the drainage or the odor-grade infill.

How much to charge for a putting green?

A putting green is not landscape turf with a tighter cut. On the sample rates a 400-square-foot putting green on a prepared pad with 15% waste and 80 feet of seam prices around $7,107 ($17.77 per square foot, 26.1 crew-hours, 460 sq ft of turf to buy). Extra seams and a thicker base are their own tickets.

        Common questions

        What does this turf estimate include?

        The price adds up turf material for the lawn area plus roll waste, a crushed-rock base by depth, sod demo and dump weight when selected, infill bags, geotextile fabric when selected, seam tape and perimeter nails, tree wells, a permit line, travel and equipment, overhead, and your target margin — all from the turf type, area, and rates you enter, not a flat price list.

        Why does landscape, pet, and putting-green turf price differently for the same lawn?

        Each turf type starts from its own suggested hours and material rates — pet turf adds drainage hours and drainage material that landscape and putting-green turf skip, on top of a heavier turf and infill weight. The “Same lawn, three turf types” comparison prices your same takeoff under each type’s starting kit so you can see where a cheap landscape rate would lose money on a pet yard.

        Why is the turf I buy bigger than the lawn I measured?

        Turf ships in rolls that are typically 15 feet wide, so seams and cuts leave scrap on almost every job. The waste percent you enter is applied to the lawn area to get the turf you actually buy, and every line that scales with turf rather than lawn area — install labor among them — uses that larger number.

        Is my data uploaded anywhere?

        No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage between visits, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.

        What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

        The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — labor, turf, base, infill, seams, and every other line item — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

        Does this check drainage, code, or engineering requirements?

        No. Hours and material rates are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a landscaping specification, drainage design, or engineering stamp. Sod demo, geotextile fabric, and pet-turf drainage are exactly the extra costs a flat per-square-foot special leaves out, but whether a specific yard needs them is still a judgment call for the site walk.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Artificial Turf Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

"$9 a square foot installed" is not a price for a turf job — it is a price for one specific turf type, base depth, and scope, quietly applied to every yard that calls in.

What a flat rate per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote: multiply the lawn's area by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — one turf type, one base depth, a prepared pad, no sod demo, no tree wells — and then reused for every yard afterward, whether or not the next yard looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the turf type (landscape, pet/play, or putting green/sports), lawn square footage, roll waste percent, crushed-rock base depth, sod demo, perimeter and seam length, tree wells or obstacle cuts, and pet drainage, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices turf, base, sod demo, infill, seams, and drainage separately by task and turf type, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat rate per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the turf is landscape, pet, or putting green — even though pet turf alone adds drainage hours, drainage material, and heavier infill that landscape turf never sees. Prices turf, infill, and drainage per turf type, so landscape, pet, and putting green are never quoted off the same number.
Has no line for sod demo, regardless of whether the existing lawn has to be stripped, hauled, and dumped before turf goes down. Prices sod-demo hours and dump-ton weight directly, so a job with an existing lawn to remove costs more than one on a prepared pad.
Prices the lawn's measured square footage, with no separate line for the roll waste that turf's 15-foot width always leaves on the cutting-room floor. Applies your waste percent to the lawn area to get the turf you actually have to buy, and prices install labor and turf material off that larger number.
Has no line for tree wells, obstacle cuts, or a deeper base, regardless of how many the yard needs. Prices tree wells per opening and base tons per inch of depth, so a yard with two tree wells and a 4-inch base costs more than the same square footage with neither.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two lawns, the same area-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets:

800 sq ft pet turf, 4 in base, sod demo, 2 tree wells$11,123.92 bid price; $7,786.75 break-even cost$7,290.86The flat rate quotes $495.89 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $3,833.06 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes use the $9.11/sq ft rate the 600 sq ft landscape job's own price works out to. Applied to the pet-turf job's 800 sq ft, that rate does not just erode margin — it prices below the job's own cost to complete. Run your own lawn's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one yard it was built for, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get a turf quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is turf type and scope, not area. Pet turf on the same footprint as landscape turf needs a heavier turf face weight, drainage hours and material, more infill, and usually a deeper base -- and a job with sod demo or tree wells adds hours and dump weight a landscape-only job never sees. A flat per-square-foot rate charges all of that the same as a bare pad on a prepared lot.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

Sod demo, base depth, pet drainage, and tree wells or obstacle cuts. A job that needs the existing lawn stripped, hauled, and dumped, plus two tree wells cut into the turf, is doing four things a bare-pad landscape job is not -- and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a 600 sq ft landscape job with sod demo prices at $5,468.14, which works out to $9.11 a square foot. Applying that same $9.11 rate to an 800 sq ft pet-turf job with sod demo and two tree wells quotes $7,290.86 -- $495.89 below that job's own $7,786.75 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit. The flat rate does not just cut the margin on the pet job; it prices it as a loss.

Is a flat rate per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same turf type, similar base depth, no sod demo or wells either time -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which job it was built on and neither does the estimator until the takeoff is actually done.

Does this calculator know what turf or labor costs in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the turf type, lawn square footage, waste percent, base depth, sod demo, seams, tree wells, and the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Artificial Turf Bid Calculator to price your own lawn, or read the pricing walkthrough.

No warranty. This free tool is not landscaping, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a base or drainage design is adequate. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and material costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a job.

vs-jobber.html.text:
← Artificial Turf Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this artificial-turf job cost, given its square footage, base, and seams, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes lawn square footage, roll waste percent, crushed-rock base depth, perimeter and seam length, tree wells or obstacle cuts, pet drainage, and per-task labor hours for demo, base, install, infill, seaming, and drainage, plus turf, infill, gravel, and seam-tape material costs, loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money and a copyable customer-facing bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

They do different jobs, and an artificial-turf installer of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
